synthesis.headline: Season's coldest air plunges into the East as the western ridge gives way to Pacific storms
synthesis.narrative:
The story is a polar plunge. A cold front runs from the Great Lakes through the central Plains into west Texas, backed by strong November highs of 1032-1033 mb over Montana, Utah and Colorado. WPC expects the season's coldest air so far to reach much of the central and eastern US from tonight. Ahead of the front, a weak low moving from Iowa toward Indiana brings a Marginal severe risk from eastern Illinois to middle Tennessee this afternoon and evening. Damaging gusts, isolated hail and perhaps a tornado are possible, but dewpoints in the 30s to mid 40s limit instability. On Thursday a large low reaches the Mid-Atlantic coast with steady rain from the northern Mid-Atlantic to southern New England and minor high-tide flooding. Rain turns to snow in the central and southern Appalachians Thursday night. SPC forecasts no severe weather Thursday, and WPC shows no excessive-rainfall risk either day. The West stays warm, with a few near-record highs from the Pacific Northwest to the Great Basin.

At 500 mb, an amplified ridge with a closed 588 dam high over the Great Basin sits upstream of a positively tilted, open trough from the Upper Midwest to Texas. Heights are 546-558 dam at Lake Superior, with a 528-534 dam cold-core low over eastern Canada. Northwesterly flow on the ridge's east side drives the cold air south along a 55-75 kt jet band from the northern Plains to New England. Westerly low-level flow cuts off Gulf moisture, which keeps today's storms marginal. The next disruption is already visible: a 95+ kt jet streak and a deep, roughly 970 hPa low off British Columbia.

That Pacific system breaks the western ridge. Heavy rain reaches northern California and the Pacific Northwest Friday, followed by repeated rounds and lower Sierra snow levels this weekend. In the East, Saturday highs run 5-15°F below average from the Southeast to the Mid-Atlantic, with a widespread freeze from the interior Deep South to the Ohio Valley before slow moderation. A southern-stream trough could bring 1-2 inches near the Texas Gulf coast. This is a regime change, not a temporary flattening. CPC's 6-10 day heights move positive anomalies east of the Rockies, up to about +21 dam near Hudson Bay, with negative anomalies over the West Coast and Southwest. At 8-14 days the ridge core sits over the Great Lakes and Northeast. Above-normal temperatures are favored for the north-central US.
synthesis.climate_context: A strong El Niño is still strengthening. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.46 for August-October, up from +2.16, although the season-to-season gains are shrinking. This week's eastern cold plunge comes from a high-amplitude wave over the continent, not from El Niño, which usually tilts winter toward a stronger southern-stream and Pacific jet. The coming turn to West Coast storms and a southern-stream trough across Texas fits that tendency but cannot be pinned on El Niño from one week. The Atlantic hurricane season is winding down, and NHC expects no formation in the next seven days. The latest teleconnection indices are from October 31, too old to use.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active. Dry, windy air behind the front raises fire danger in the lower Mississippi Valley and central Gulf Coast Thursday. Lake-effect snow develops over the Upper Peninsula, and upslope snow falls in West Virginia and western Maryland through Saturday. In Canada, a 1042 hPa Arctic high supplies the cold air, while strong onshore flow hits the BC coast. Tropical Storm Pena (40 kt), far southwest of Hawaii, should dissipate near the Dateline by Nov 14 without affecting land.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 12Z analysis for Wednesday November 11, 2026 shows a strong continental anticyclone in the interior West, with highs of roughly 1032 mb over Montana and the northern Rockies and 1033 mb over Utah and Colorado, plus a 1030 mb center near the Idaho-Oregon area. These are legitimately strong November highs, and the closely spaced isobars along their northern and eastern flanks mark the tightest gradient on the map, extending across the northern Plains. A cold front sweeps from the Great Lakes and southern Ontario southwestward through the central Plains and into west Texas, with a 1009 mb low near the Iowa-Minnesota-Illinois area, a stationary or warm-front segment (red semicircles) extending east of it toward the Great Lakes, and a 1013 mb low farther northeast near Ontario and Quebec. Another cold front pushes through the Pacific Northwest along the far left edge of the domain, and a front trails down the East Coast near a 1015 mb low off the Mid-Atlantic and Carolina coast.

Gradients are slack across the Southeast, where a weak 1018 mb high near Georgia and the Carolinas sits under light winds, and over the southern Plains and Gulf Coast. A 1020 mb high over south Texas is similarly modest and explains little beyond light flow there.

Lift and moisture are focused along the central Plains cold front and around the Upper Midwest low, where the boundary meets the warm-front segment, with a second focus near the East Coast low and its attendant front. Behind the Plains front, the large cold-air mass is spreading south and east beneath the western highs. Without upper-air data on this chart, the precipitation potential along these boundaries is only implied by the frontal geometry and the low centers.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This is the CMC surface analysis valid 00Z Wednesday 11 November 2026, on a polar projection where the upper frame is the Arctic Ocean, the Canadian Archipelago and Greenland, so the strongest circulation over land is the low near 970 hPa at lower left of center, which I place over the northeast Pacific and the British Columbia coast, with the coastline nearby making that the likeliest reading. A trailing cold front and a longer front curving southwest from it sweep out over the Pacific, and a second occluded system near 987 hPa sits further west, with the tightest isobar packing between these lows and the high near 1031 to the south. Isobars also crowd along the Pacific side of the 970 low, which implies a strong onshore flow, though the chart plots no winds beyond station barbs I cannot read reliably.

Downstream, a 973 hPa low sits inland over what appears to be northern British Columbia or the Yukon-Alberta area, ahead of the main center; I am less sure of its exact province because the border lines are faint. A frontal trough runs southeast from the 1000 hPa low near the center of the frame, through the western Arctic and Prairies sector, and continues as a cold front toward the Great Lakes and the central United States, where it connects to a weaker 1013 hPa low and a 1015 hPa low near the lower middle of the chart. This is the clearest cross-border link: a cold front stretching from the Canadian interior into the US Midwest.

To the east, a 996 hPa low near the middle right, around Hudson Bay or the surrounding Shield, and a 993 hPa low further east near Labrador and the Atlantic coast carry fronts, including an occluded and trailing cold front hooking south over the Maritimes and Atlantic waters. The deepest low on the chart, roughly 984 hPa at far upper right, sits over the high Arctic and Greenland area, not southern Canada, so its depth is ordinary for November at that latitude.

Strong ridging dominates the Arctic interior, with a 1042 hPa high near the Archipelago and Greenland side and several 1031 to 1032 hPa highs, giving a broad, cold, dry high-pressure cap over the north. Over the southern US, weak highs near 1024 to 1027 hPa support light gradients, in sharp contrast to the tight gradients along the Pacific coast.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The pattern is a classic amplified western ridge with a broad eastern trough, valid 1200 UTC 11 Nov 2026. Heights over the Intermountain West and Four Corners sit near 584-588 dam, with a closed high contour (roughly 588) around the Great Basin and southern Rockies, while the contours dive sharply southward over the central Plains and Mississippi Valley, where the 546-558 dam heights seen at Lake Superior and the Upper Midwest give way to the 570s over the Gulf Coast states. A second, cold-core low sits in the northeast corner of the chart over eastern Canada, with 528-534 dam heights and a closed circulation near the plotted L, so the eastern pattern is trough-dominated with the strongest height gradient in the Great Lakes and Northeast.

The trough axis tilts positively, running from the Upper Midwest southwestward through the central Plains toward Texas, with the 570-576 dam contours kinking along that line. No closed low is evident over the CONUS itself; the open-wave trough continues to ride the westerlies, so it will translate eastward rather than pivot in place. The closed contours near the Pacific Northwest and the northwestern corner of the chart are tied to the strong cold-air region plotted there (the red shading marks winds above 85 kt), but the chart edge cuts off the full structure, so I would not call that a cutoff.

The strongest winds appear in two places: the upper-left corner over the Pacific and British Columbia, where the 95+ kt shading suggests a jet streak entering from the west, and a band from the northern Plains through the Great Lakes into New England, where 55-75 kt shading (the olive-to-yellow range) marks the implied jet corridor around the trough base and eastern flank. A weaker 40-55 kt maximum is plotted along the Gulf Coast and Southeast coast, consistent with southwesterly flow ahead of the trough.

Because the western ridge is placed upstream of the eastern trough in a wave-like sequence with no distinct cutoff low beneath a poleward high, this is not a Rex block. It is a high-amplitude but still progressive pattern: a quasi-stationary western ridge feeding northwesterly flow into a trough that is translating east, with the Plains-to-Northeast jet providing the forcing. The pattern favors a sharp temperature contrast, with cold air plunging southward behind the trough axis and unseasonably warm conditions beneath the western ridge, though I cannot assess anomalies from absolute heights alone.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 13:21Z on 11 November shows a sharp airmass boundary running from the southern Plains northeastward across the Mississippi and Ohio Valleys into the Great Lakes, with green tropical-moist air to its south and blue-green, cooler and drier upper-level air to its north. The sharpest contrast along this edge, roughly from Texas and Oklahoma through Arkansas and Tennessee and onward toward Lake Michigan, marks the likely jet corridor, though no isotachs are plotted to pin an axis. A narrow orange-brown dry streamer follows this boundary from northern Mexico across Texas and the Gulf coastal states toward the Carolinas, consistent with a baroclinic zone with dry upper-level air on its cool side.

A darker, curved dry signature arcs through eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin around the western and southern flank of the cloud mass over Lake Michigan and the Great Lakes, suggesting a trough or closed circulation there. The comma-shaped cloud band extending from Illinois and Lake Michigan east-northeastward across Ontario and the Great Lakes is the primary cloud signature of that system. The broad red and brown tones over Ontario, Quebec and the Canadian Maritimes are dry upper-tropospheric air. Because they sit near cyclonic flow rather than under a ridge, some stratospheric influence is plausible, but the broad, diffuse character argues against reading it as a compact intrusion.

Over the northwestern United States and the eastern Pacific, a bright cloud shield and a purple-blue gradient along the upper-left limb point to a separate, strongly cold and dry upper-level system approaching the Pacific Northwest, though limb distortion makes fine detail unreliable. The Southeast is mostly clear to partly cloudy, with a moderate cloud mass over Alabama and Georgia. The most vigorous deep convection, shown as bright white, compact tops, sits over the northwestern Caribbean south of Cuba, near the Cayman and Jamaica area, and in the western Atlantic east of Florida and north of the Greater Antilles, with a further cluster over the southwestern Caribbean off the coast of Central America. A band of cloud also extends along the Texas coast and the western Gulf, consistent with moisture overrunning the stalled frontal zone.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 13:10Z on 11 November shows a broad band of purple, blue and white across Canada and the high latitudes, marking cold, dry upper-tropospheric air on the poleward side of the flow. The sharp color contrast between that cold air and the greener subtropical air over the northern US implies a polar-jet corridor running across southern Canada and the Great Lakes toward the Northeast, with cloud shields along it. Over the western North Atlantic east of New England and the Canadian Maritimes, a curved white cloud band with an adjacent dark brown to red patch suggests a mature system; the dry air wrapping into its southwest flank is consistent with a stratospheric-intrusion signature, though a cutoff versus open trough cannot be confirmed from color alone.

The tropics are dominated by green moist air, with the largest convective clusters (bright white) over Central America and the western Caribbean, from the Yucatán and Honduras region eastward toward Cuba and Hispaniola, and scattered cells near the Bahamas and Florida peninsula. The pattern fits the late-season ITCZ and Caribbean convection, but no organized circulation or tropical cyclone is evident at this scale. In the eastern Pacific, white convective clouds cluster west of Ecuador and Colombia near the equator and in the far-west edge of the disk, with broad olive-green (moist) air between them.

Over South America, scattered convective clouds sit over the western Amazon basin and southern Brazil, with a larger comma-shaped cloud mass near Uruguay and the adjacent Atlantic suggesting a frontal system there. Further south, the southeast Pacific near the southern Chile coast shows swirled cloud and warm-toned dry air, consistent with a mid-latitude cyclone and a possible dry-intrusion wrap. Strongly saturated orange-red patches along the far-western and far-southern limb should be read cautiously, since view-angle effects stretch the colors there.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This 6-10 day outlook for November 16-20, 2026 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the country, with the strongest signal over the Upper Midwest. The darkest shading, 80-90% odds of above normal, covers Minnesota and the eastern Dakotas, with 70-80% extending through Iowa, Nebraska, Wisconsin and northern Missouri, and 60-70% reaching into Kansas, Oklahoma, Illinois, Indiana and Michigan. Probabilities step down fairly uniformly toward the edges: 40-50% across the northern Rockies and interior Northwest, and 33-40% over parts of the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic and New England.

The cool signal is confined to California and western Nevada, where a core of 40-50% odds of below normal is ringed by 33-40%, with a smaller 33-40% below-normal area along the Carolina coast. Near-normal (equal chances) covers the Pacific Northwest coast, the Great Basin and Southwest, and a swath from Georgia and Florida north through the central Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic. Alaska leans above normal, strongest in the east, and Hawaii is also favored above.

Note that these are probabilities of terciles, not magnitudes, so the 80-90% area says the models agree on warmth, not that the departures are extreme. The tight gradient from the Plains toward the Pacific Coast is consistent with a western trough or cutoff low off California under a broad central-U.S. ridge, but the chart does not show heights, so that is an implied pattern. If that reading holds, the outlook suggests persistence rather than breakdown through day 10, with the cool-western, warm-central dipole intact. The sharp northeast-southwest-oriented transition from warm to near-normal along the Appalachians and East Coast hints at a trough or frontal zone lingering near the Atlantic seaboard, which is where any pattern change would most likely show first.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook, made 10 Nov 2026 and valid 16-20 Nov. Contour labels are plotted in meters (5160, 5400, 5820, etc.), equivalent to roughly 516 to 582 dam, and the dashed anomaly lines are at 60 m intervals, so the labels of 60, 120, 180 and 210 are meters, i.e. 6 to 21 dam. The strongest positive center sits over the Canadian Arctic and Hudson Bay region, where a ridge extends north from the central US into the Arctic, with anomalies up to about +21 dam and several red dashed rings around it. A second, weaker positive area covers the eastern US and the western Atlantic seaboard, with anomalies labeled near +9 to +21 dam. The negative centers are the large trough over Alaska and the Bering Sea side of the domain, and an elongated trough along the west coast, with the lower anomaly line near -12 dam; the west-coast trough also shows a closed -12 dam region over the Southwest, reaching toward the northern Mexico border.

The chart shows the ridge axis running from the Gulf Coast and Mississippi Valley north across the Great Lakes toward Baffin Island and Greenland, so the positive anomalies are centered east of the Rockies rather than over western North America. The zero-anomaly line (purple) runs roughly down the West Coast and across the interior West, meaning western North America is mostly under negative anomalies, with positive anomalies confined to the eastern two-thirds of the continent. The contours bow strongly poleward from the central US into the Arctic, a high-amplitude, meridional pattern rather than zonal flow, with the Alaska-to-West Coast trough and the downstream ridge both clearly defined.

Since this is a single ensemble-mean map with no comparison to an earlier outlook, whether the western positive anomalies are holding or retreating cannot be read from this image alone. What the chart does support is that, by days 6-10, positive anomalies have been displaced east of the western cordillera, with troughing favored over Alaska and the West Coast.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and departures outlook (made Nov 10, valid Nov 18-24, 2026), a polar stereographic view of North America. The green contours are mean heights labeled in meters (5160 to 5880 m, i.e. roughly 516 to 588 dam), and the dashed lines are departures from normal at 60 m intervals; the 60 m interval and the plotted labels are in meters, so a labeled "120" or "90" is 120 or 90 m (12 or 9 dam), not decameters.

The dominant positive anomaly is a broad area of red dashed contours centered over the eastern Great Lakes and Northeast, extending into southeastern Canada and the Atlantic coast, with the labeled 90 value near the central Great Lakes and a closed center farther east near the Maritimes. A second positive area of red contours sits over the Alaska and Yukon sector in the upper left. Negative anomalies (blue dashed) fill the eastern Pacific off the West Coast and a separate area to the north near Baffin Island and Greenland, where the labels 120 and 90 appear, with another negative center over the Southwest and northern Mexico.

On the chart as drawn, I do not see a positive anomaly over western Canada, the northern Rockies, or the northern Plains. That region sits between the eastern ridge and the Pacific trough, with contours running from southwest to northeast, and the blue negative contours lie to its west. The ridge core is therefore well to the east, over the Great Lakes and Northeast, with an axis oriented roughly from the Gulf Coast toward Hudson Bay.

The trough axis lies over the eastern Pacific and the West Coast, producing southwesterly flow across the Rockies and the central US. The tightly packed height contours across the northern tier, from the Pacific Northwest to Hudson Bay, imply a strong westerly to southwesterly flow, with the implied jet corridor running through that gradient.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary: This Day 1 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Wednesday November 11 through 12Z Thursday November 12, 2026, shows no risk areas drawn anywhere on the map. The text across the central United States states that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent, which is below the threshold of the lowest category, Marginal (at least 5 percent). None of the Marginal, Slight, Moderate or High categories appear over any state or coastline, so there is no highest-risk area to identify. With nothing outlined, the chart gives no indication of a tropical system, stalled front or terrain-enhanced heavy rain threatening flash flooding during this 24-hour period. This is a statement about flash-flood potential only; ordinary rain or snow could still occur without being heavy enough to exceed flash flood guidance.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: No risk area is drawn on this Day 2 outlook, valid 12Z Thursday November 12 to 12Z Friday November 13, 2026. The map is blank across the contiguous United States, with a text note stating that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent. That means none of the legend categories (Marginal, Slight, Moderate or High) are depicted anywhere, so there is no shaded corridor over the Gulf Coast, Southeast, Mississippi Valley, Plains or any other region. The chart gives no basis for comparing against a Day 1 outlook, so I can't say whether the risk has grown, shifted or relaxed. It only shows that, as of the 0805Z issuance on November 11, forecasters saw no meaningful excessive-rainfall threat nationwide for this period. That does not rule out ordinary rain or local ponding, since the product addresses only flash-flood-level exceedances, and it carries no information about rainfall totals.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: As of 300 AM EST Wednesday, November 11, 2026 (valid through 12Z Friday, November 13), the WPC forecast calls for an anomalous polar plunge bringing the season's coldest air so far to much of the central and eastern U.S. from Wednesday night. A front with showers and storms crosses the Midwest, Ohio Valley, and Tennessee Valley Wednesday into Wednesday night, with some storms in the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys capable of damaging wind gusts. A large low reaches the Mid-Atlantic coast Thursday, bringing steady rain from northern Mid-Atlantic to southern New England, increasing coastal winds, and minor coastal flooding at high tides. Rain changes to snow over the central and southern Appalachians Thursday night, with wet snow possible in interior New England. Lake-effect snow develops over the Upper Peninsula. Freezes reach Tennessee and the southern Appalachians by Friday morning, with a widespread hard freeze into the South over the weekend. Dry, windy conditions raise fire danger in the lower Mississippi Valley and central Gulf Coast Thursday. In the West, unseasonable warmth and a few near-record highs persist from the Pacific Northwest into the Great Basin, and heavy rain reaches northern California and the Pacific Northwest Friday morning.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
As of the 0655 AM CST Wednesday, November 11, 2026 issuance (valid 13Z November 11 to 12Z November 12), the Storm Prediction Center has a Marginal Risk of severe thunderstorms from eastern Illinois into Indiana, western and central Kentucky, and middle Tennessee. Threats are isolated hail, damaging winds, and perhaps a tornado, mainly this afternoon and evening.

A mid-level shortwave is digging over the Upper Midwest toward the mid Mississippi Valley, with a weak surface low moving from southeast Iowa toward Indiana by late afternoon. A cold front is advancing east-southeast across the southern Plains, mid-Mississippi Valley, and lower Ohio Valley. The main limiting factor is shallow low-level moisture, with surface dewpoints in the 30s to mid 40s and only weak MLCAPE. Westerly low-level flow is expected to keep richer Gulf-region moisture from reaching the area. Storms should first develop over eastern Illinois around 18-21Z, with 30-40 kt of deep-layer shear, and the severe threat should wane this evening as instability diminishes.

Across the central and southern Florida Peninsula, isolated to scattered sea-breeze thunderstorms may produce small hail and gusty winds, though multiple inversions aloft should limit updraft strength.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours. No organized convective threat is currently being actively monitored by the Storm Prediction Center. No specific systems, locations, or risk areas are under active watch in this product.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic (as of 700 AM EST Wednesday, November 11, 2026): Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the North Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, or Gulf of America during the next 7 days.

East Pacific (as of 400 AM PST Wednesday, November 11, 2026): The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical Storm Pena, located several hundred miles southwest of Honolulu, Hawaii. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 longitude during the next 7 days.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
Tropical Storm Pena (Advisory 19, as of 2026-11-11 09:00 UTC, or 11 PM HST Tuesday, Nov 10) is centered near 10.1N 166.7W, about 495 miles SSE of Johnston Island and 970 miles SW of Honolulu. Maximum sustained winds are 45 mph (40 kt) with higher gusts, and the estimated minimum central pressure is 1002 mb. Tropical-storm-force winds extend up to 115 miles from the center, mostly north of it. Pena is moving west (260 degrees) near 9 mph.

No coastal watches or warnings are in effect, and no hazards are expected to affect land. The next complete advisory is due at 5 AM HST.

Forecasters expect the storm to continue west for the next few days, accelerating under a subtropical ridge to the north. The track has shifted slightly south, close to a blend of the Google DeepMind ensemble and HFIP Corrected Consensus guidance.

Intensity is forecast to hold at 40 kt through 24 hours, then weaken to 35 kt by 36 hours and 30 kt by 60 hours. Westerly shear and a small increase in shear and drying by Thursday are expected to drive the weakening. Pena is forecast to dissipate by 72 hours (around 06 UTC Nov 14) near the International Dateline, either from persistent unfavorable conditions or from increased forward speed that opens the system into a trough. Forecast positions are 10.0N 168.4W at 12 hours, 10.2N 171.2W at 24 hours, 10.6N 174.3W at 36 hours, 11.0N 177.4W at 48 hours, and 11.4N 179.5E at 60 hours.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary:
The Oceanic Niño Index shows a strong and still-strengthening El Niño in the equatorial Pacific. The seasonal anomaly has risen every season in the table, from -0.21 in JFM 2026 (near neutral, slightly cool) to +2.46 in ASO 2026, the latest value. That is well above the +0.5 El Niño threshold and in the strong (+2.0 and above) range.

The anomaly climbed steadily from late winter into summer: +0.11 (FMA), +0.46 (MAM), +0.95 (AMJ), +1.39 (MJJ), +1.80 (JJA), +2.16 (JAS). The rate of increase has slowed somewhat in the most recent seasons, with gains of +0.36 (JAS) and +0.30 (ASO), though the index is still rising.

The TOTAL column, the base-period sea surface temperature, rose from 26.57 to 29.23 over the same period, tracking the warming trend. The table gives no issue date, so the currency of these values cannot be confirmed from the product.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices from NOAA CPC, observed values, as of 2026-10-31. The table is flagged STALE: the newest value is 11 days old and CPC has not updated it, so these should not be treated as current.

PNA: latest +0.57, after a low of about -0.58 earlier in the window and a sharp rebound over the last three days. The 7-day mean is -0.24, down from +0.06 the prior week. Positive values favor western North American ridging with eastern troughing.

AO: latest +0.77, still positive but drifting down from a peak near +2.78 early in the window. The 7-day mean is +1.03, down from +1.44. Positive values argue against high-latitude blocking.

NAO: latest +1.15, rising. The 7-day mean is +0.59, up from +0.26. The index was negative (near -0.79) mid-window before recovering.

These are observed values, and extratropical teleconnections are weaker outside winter. Treat them as directional support only.
